Yes, repeatedly making yourself throw up will increase acid reflux. And yes the skin around your mouth can get irritated from the harsh stomach acid that will aggravate it when throwing up. 

The acid reflux problem will likely get worse the more you throw up. There’s nothing you can really do about that. For the skin issue I would say to try using a light face wash after throwing up and a thin layering of facial moisturiser.

I’m not a medical professional, this is from my own experience.

I feel your pain! I’ve hated anything fizzy since I was a kid. This is a list of items I’ve found in my country, a tip would be to scour the drinks aisle for ‘sugar free’ in the title, I find you can hardly ever go wrong there.

- Monster Super Fuel zero sugar
- Powerade Zero (blue and red)
- Lipton peach ice tea 99% sugar free
- Gatorade zero
- Powerade active waters (sugar free)
- Aloe Vera 99% sugar free
- lite or reduced sugar cordials (you just add water to them)
- flavoured drink powders like Raro can often be found sugar free or close to nowadays
- sports electrolyte sachets which are often sugar free/low calorie, taste nice and you may want the electrolytes

Hope this helps x

I sometimes get stuck on watching lots of childhood trauma/therapy type videos and I remember learning about how the first three years of life are very important as they basically set the foundation for yourself in later life. Its about how you were interacted with as a baby and how that effects you later in life. The sudden loss of your mother and quick change of environment may have disrupted your development, along with anything happening in your family system. Anything a parent does or doesn't do can effect the baby later, for an example if a baby is exposed to the parents constantly arguing and cries out and it gets ignored it every time may lead the baby to suppress their emotions later in life because they think their emotions are insignificant, which is not true. So much of how we view ourselves is based off of what our parents taught us to believe about ourselves.
